Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers with a fixed, finite number of significant bits, typically following the IEEE 754 standard. When two floating-point numbers are added, the hardware must align their exponents, add the significands, and then round the result back to the representable precision. This rounding step discards information whenever the exact mathematical sum cannot be represented exactly, which is the common case. Because rounding depends on the specific values being combined at each step, the order in which numbers are summed determines which intermediate values get rounded and by how much. Consequently, (a + b) + c can produce a different result than a + (b + c), even though these are mathematically identical, because the intermediate sum a + b or b + c may round differently, and that rounding error propagates differently through the rest of the computation. This is a well-known and unavoidable consequence of finite-precision arithmetic, not a bug or hardware defect.

This lack of associativity becomes especially significant in large matrix multiplications, where each output element is computed as a sum of many products, often thousands or millions of terms in deep learning or scientific computing contexts. The order in which these products are summed, known as the reduction order, is not fixed by the mathematical definition of matrix multiplication; it is determined by the implementation. Different hardware architectures, libraries, or even different runs on the same hardware can sum these terms in different orders due to parallelization strategies, tiling schemes, use of multiple threads or GPU cores, vectorized instructions, or fused multiply-add operations. A CPU might accumulate in a straightforward sequential order, while a GPU might split the reduction across many cores and combine partial sums in a tree-like fashion, and different libraries may choose different tile sizes or blocking strategies that change the grouping of additions.

As a result, running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, or even with different threading configurations on the same hardware, can yield results that differ in the least significant bits. For a single multiplication this difference is usually negligible, but in large-scale computations such as training deep neural networks, where millions of matrix multiplications are chained together and outputs feed into subsequent operations, these tiny discrepancies can accumulate and amplify, especially through nonlinear operations or iterative processes. This makes bitwise reproducibility across different hardware, software versions, or parallelization schemes difficult to guarantee, even when the underlying algorithm and mathematical formulation remain unchanged, and it is a central reason why reproducing exact numerical results across systems requires careful control over execution order, not just algorithmic equivalence.

Floating-point numbers represent a finite subset of the reals: each value has a fixed-width significand, so most results of arithmetic must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition in IEEE 754 is defined as the exact mathematical sum followed by a single rounding, which makes the operation commutative but not associative, because the rounding applied after each partial sum discards information that a different grouping would have retained. The classic illustration involves a large value and two small ones: if you add a very large number to a tiny number, the tiny number may fall entirely below the least significant bit of the large one and vanish, so adding it twice separately loses both contributions, whereas adding the two tiny numbers to each other first can produce a quantity large enough to survive the final rounding. Cancellation produces the mirror image of the problem: subtracting two nearly equal numbers exposes low-order bits whose accuracy depends on how the earlier partial sums were rounded, so the relative error in the final result can be enormous even though every individual operation was correctly rounded to within half an ulp. Extended-precision accumulators, fused multiply-add, and vector instructions change where roundings occur but do not restore associativity; they merely shift the error pattern.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and every dot product is a reduction, so this sensitivity is structural rather than incidental. A high-performance implementation almost never accumulates a dot product in index order. It blocks the computation for cache and register reuse, splits the reduction dimension into tiles, accumulates several partial sums in separate vector lanes, and combines them in a tree at the end. It may split the reduction across threads or across GPU thread blocks and combine the pieces with atomics, in which case the order depends on runtime scheduling and is not even fixed from run to run on the same machine. Consequently the same mathematical product computed with a different tile size, a different number of threads, a different vector width, a different library version, or a different accelerator generally yields results that differ in the last few bits. Those differences are individually tiny but they propagate: in an iterative solver or a deep network they can be amplified by ill-conditioning, alter a comparison or a branch, change which pivot is selected, or shift a training trajectory so that final metrics diverge visibly. Reproducibility therefore requires pinning the reduction order explicitly, using deterministic kernels, or accepting agreement only to a documented tolerance rather than bitwise identity.

Floating-point numbers are represented with a fixed number of significant bits, so every arithmetic operation—especially addition—must round its result to fit back into that representation. This rounding is the root cause of non-associativity. When we compute (a + b) + c, the machine first adds a and b, rounds that intermediate sum to the nearest representable value, and then adds c and rounds again. If instead we compute a + (b + c), the intermediate rounding happens at a different point, on a different pair of values, and can produce a different intermediate result. Because rounding is a nonlinear, discontinuous operation, these two rounding paths do not generally converge to the same final answer. The discrepancy is usually tiny, on the order of the machine epsilon, but it is real and it accumulates as more terms are summed.

Modern hardware makes this issue unavoidable rather than incidental. CPUs and GPUs exploit parallelism through vectorized SIMD units, multiple cores, and thread scheduling that is often nondeterministic in the order threads complete. Fused multiply-add instructions, different instruction sets, and compiler optimizations that reorder or reassociate expressions for performance all change the order in which partial sums are formed. Libraries like BLAS or cuBLAS choose reduction strategies—tree reductions, blocked summation, warp-level shuffles—based on hardware architecture, tile sizes, and thread counts, and these choices can differ between runs, between library versions, or between different GPU models entirely.

In matrix multiplication, each output element is a dot product, i.e., a sum of many products, so it is directly exposed to this effect. Large matrices used in deep learning or scientific computing may involve dot products with thousands of terms. The particular sequence in which those products are accumulated—determined by tiling strategy, thread block size, memory layout, or even whether the kernel launches with a different number of streaming multiprocessors—changes the rounding trajectory and thus the least significant bits of the result. Running the same multiplication on the same input twice, but on different hardware, different library versions, or even a different number of threads on the same GPU, can yield bitwise-different outputs, even though both are “correct” to within floating-point tolerance.

This matters for reproducibility because many scientific and machine-learning workflows expect bit-identical results across runs for debugging, auditing, or verifying training determinism. Achieving true bitwise reproducibility on such systems requires deliberately fixing the reduction order—for example forcing sequential summation or using deterministic reduction algorithms—at a cost in performance, since much of the hardware’s speed advantage comes precisely from exploiting the freedom to reassociate.

Floating-point addition is not associative because floating-point numbers have finite precision, and every arithmetic operation on them is rounded to fit back into that limited representation. When you add two floating-point numbers, the exact mathematical result may require more significant bits than the format allows, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. This rounding step depends on the relative magnitudes and signs of the operands being combined at that moment. Because of this, (a + b) + c can produce a different rounded result than a + (b + c), since the intermediate value a + b or b + c may already have discarded information that affects how the final addition rounds. In exact real-number arithmetic these two groupings are identical, but in finite-precision arithmetic the order in which partial sums are formed changes which digits get truncated or rounded away, and this can propagate into different final answers, especially when the values being summed vary widely in magnitude.

This property becomes significant in large matrix multiplications because computing each output element requires summing many products, and the summation order is not fixed by the mathematical definition of matrix multiplication—it's a choice made by the implementation. Modern hardware, including multi-core CPUs and GPUs, computes these sums using parallel reduction trees, blocked or tiled accumulation strategies, or vectorized instructions that process multiple partial sums simultaneously before combining them. The exact grouping of additions depends on the number of threads, the tile size, the order of memory access, the specific hardware architecture, and even the compiler or library version. Different GPUs, different numbers of CUDA cores in use, or different BLAS libraries may all choose different but mathematically equivalent reduction orders.

As a consequence, running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, or even the same hardware with different batch sizes, thread configurations, or library versions, can yield numerically different results at the level of the least significant bits. These differences are usually tiny in isolation, but in deep learning training, iterative numerical algorithms, or any pipeline where many operations compound over time, they can amplify into meaningfully different outputs, gradients, or final model weights. This makes bitwise reproducibility across different hardware or software configurations difficult to guarantee, and it's why frameworks that require strict reproducibility often need to fix the reduction algorithm, disable certain parallel optimizations, or use deterministic kernels, accepting a potential performance cost in exchange for consistent, repeatable numerical results across runs.

Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers with a finite number of significant bits, forcing every arithmetic operation to round its result to the nearest representable value. When we add two floating-point numbers, the exact mathematical sum often cannot be represented exactly, so the hardware rounds it according to a fixed rule, typically round-to-nearest-even in IEEE 754 arithmetic. The consequence is that (a + b) + c can produce a different rounded result than a + (b + c), because the intermediate rounding errors introduced at each step depend on the order in which values are combined. In exact real-number arithmetic these two expressions are identical, but in floating-point arithmetic the rounding that occurs after the first addition changes the bits that are fed into the second addition, and that can shift which direction the final rounding goes. This is not a flaw or bug in the hardware; it is an unavoidable consequence of representing a continuum of real numbers with a finite binary encoding.

This property becomes practically significant in large matrix multiplications, where each output element is computed as a sum of many products. Mathematically, the order in which these products are summed does not matter, but numerically it does, because each partial sum is rounded before the next term is added. Modern hardware introduces many possible reduction orders: multi-threaded CPUs may split the sum across cores and combine partial results in an order that depends on thread scheduling; GPUs use parallel reduction trees, warp-level shuffles, and tensor cores that accumulate in specific, often nondeterministic, orders depending on how work is scheduled across streaming multiprocessors; and libraries may choose different blocking or tiling strategies depending on matrix size, cache behavior, or available hardware features. Each of these choices changes the sequence in which floating-point additions occur, and because addition is not associative, the final result can differ in the last few bits, or occasionally more significantly if there is catastrophic cancellation or a wide range of magnitudes among the summed values.

For most applications, these tiny discrepancies are harmless, since they lie within the expected numerical error of floating-point computation. However, they undermine bit-for-bit reproducibility: running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, different library versions, different thread counts, or even different times with dynamic scheduling can yield slightly different numerical outputs. This matters in contexts like scientific computing, deep learning training where small differences can compound over many iterations, and any regulated or safety-critical domain where exact reproducibility of results is required for validation, debugging, or auditing purposes.

Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers with a finite number of bits, and every arithmetic operation must round its result to fit into that fixed representation. When you add two floating-point numbers, the exact mathematical sum may require more precision than the format allows, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. This rounding is what breaks associativity: for real numbers, (a + b) + c always equals a + (b + c), but for floating-point numbers, the order in which intermediate roundings occur can produce different final results. If a and b are close in magnitude but c is many orders of magnitude smaller, adding a and b first may preserve c's contribution reasonably well, whereas adding b and c first could round c away entirely before it ever gets combined with a. The rounding error introduced at each step depends on the relative magnitudes of the operands at that moment, and since those magnitudes depend on the order of operations, different orders yield different rounding errors and therefore different final sums.

This has direct consequences for large matrix multiplications, because computing a single output element of a matrix product involves summing many products, and that sum is a reduction operation. On modern hardware, this reduction can be performed in many different orders depending on how the computation is parallelized: the number of threads, the tile or block size used in a GPU kernel, the order in which a compiler or library chooses to vectorize the loop, or the specific hardware architecture and its SIMD width all influence the sequence in which partial sums are accumulated. Because floating-point addition is not associative, these different reduction orders generally produce numerically different results, even though they are all valid implementations of the same mathematical operation and even though the differences are usually tiny, on the order of machine epsilon times some accumulated factor.

The practical effect is that running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, with a different number of threads, or even the same hardware but a different library version or kernel scheduling can produce bit-wise different outputs. This makes exact reproducibility difficult in deep learning training, scientific computing, and any workflow that demands deterministic results across runs or platforms. Achieving true bitwise reproducibility usually requires forcing a fixed, deterministic reduction order, avoiding certain fast parallel reduction algorithms, or using higher-precision accumulation, all of which can trade off some performance for the guarantee of consistent results across executions.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so most real values cannot be stored exactly. A double-precision number carries roughly fifteen to seventeen significant decimal digits, and any arithmetic result that needs more precision than that must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition itself is correctly rounded on IEEE 754 hardware, meaning the machine computes the exact sum of its two inputs and then rounds once. The trouble is that rounding happens after every individual operation, and the amount of information discarded depends on the magnitudes of the operands involved. When a very small number is added to a very large one, the small number's low-order bits fall off the end of the significand and vanish entirely. Whether those bits survive long enough to matter depends on the order in which sums are accumulated.

A classic illustration uses the values one, plus a tiny epsilon just below the resolution of one, and minus one. Adding one to epsilon returns exactly one, because epsilon is too small to register, so subtracting one afterward yields zero. Group the operations differently, subtracting one from one first, and the result is epsilon. Both computations are individually correct in the sense that each addition was properly rounded, yet they disagree. Associativity fails not because the hardware is sloppy but because rounding is a nonlinear operation that does not commute with regrouping. Catastrophic cancellation, where two nearly equal large numbers subtract to leave a small difference dominated by earlier rounding error, magnifies the discrepancy dramatically.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a vast collection of dot products, and a dot product is a reduction — a sequence of additions whose grouping is an implementation choice, not part of the mathematical definition. A naive sequential loop accumulates left to right. A vectorized kernel maintains several partial sums in separate registers and combines them at the end. A blocked or tiled implementation splits the summation index into chunks, computes partial results, and adds those. A multithreaded or GPU implementation partitions the reduction across cores, and the order in which partial results arrive and merge may depend on scheduling, thread counts, or hardware occupancy. Each of these yields a different grouping of the same additions, hence a different pattern of rounding, hence numerically different output.

The practical consequence is that identical mathematical inputs can produce bitwise different matrices depending on library version, thread count, tile size, whether fused multiply-add is used, or which accelerator ran the job. Differences are typically small relative to the norm, but they can grow through repeated multiplications in iterative solvers or deep networks, and they break bitwise-exact regression tests. Achieving reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order or using compensated summation, both of which cost performance.

Floating-point numbers represent only a finite subset of the reals: each value carries a sign, an exponent, and a fixed-width significand, so most arithmetic results must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition is therefore not exact but "add, then round," and rounding depends on the magnitudes of the operands involved. When you add two numbers of very different scale, the smaller one's low-order bits fall off the end of the significand and are discarded. Whether those bits are discarded depends on what has already been accumulated, and that in turn depends on the order of operations. A canonical illustration in IEEE 754 double precision uses the values 1, 2^53, and −2^53. Adding 1 to 2^53 first yields 2^53 again, because 2^53 + 1 is not representable and rounds back down; subtracting 2^53 then gives zero. Grouping the two large values together first gives exactly zero, and adding 1 gives 1. The same three operands, the same operator, two different answers. Associativity fails not because the hardware is sloppy but because rounding is a nonlinear, magnitude-dependent operation, and the standard prescribes it deterministically for each individual operation rather than for expressions as a whole.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, and a dot product is a summation whose order is entirely a matter of implementation convenience. A naive triple loop accumulates in index order in a single register. A blocked or tiled implementation splits each dot product into partial sums over cache-sized panels and combines them at the end. A vectorized kernel keeps several independent accumulators, one per SIMD lane, and reduces them pairwise at the close. A multithreaded or multi-GPU implementation splits the reduction dimension across workers and sums their contributions in whatever order they finish, or in a tree. Every one of these schemes computes a mathematically identical sum and a numerically different one, differing in the last few bits of the mantissa, with the discrepancy growing roughly with the square root of the reduction length for random data and much faster when there is catastrophic cancellation or a wide dynamic range of terms.

The practical consequences are familiar to anyone who has chased a nondeterministic test failure. Changing the thread count, the tile size, the target architecture, the library version, or the fusion decisions of a compiler can alter results without any change to the source program. Fused multiply-add makes this worse by skipping an intermediate rounding, so a kernel that uses FMA and one that does not will disagree even at identical order. Small discrepancies then amplify through iterative solvers, comparisons against thresholds, or the training of neural networks, where a bit-level difference in one gradient can send two runs down visibly divergent trajectories. Bitwise reproducibility, when it is required, must be engineered deliberately: fixing the reduction tree, using deterministic library modes, or accumulating in higher precision or with compensated and exact summation techniques, each at some cost in speed.

Floating-point numbers can only represent a finite set of values with finite precision, so every arithmetic operation on them may need to round its result to the nearest representable number. Addition in particular loses information whenever the two operands have very different magnitudes, because the smaller number's low-order bits fall below the precision that can be represented once it is aligned to the exponent of the larger number. This rounding depends on the exact sequence of intermediate values that arise during a computation, and this is why (a + b) + c is not guaranteed to equal a + (b + c) in floating point, even though the two expressions are algebraically identical in real number arithmetic. The order in which values are summed changes the intermediate magnitudes, changes when and how rounding occurs, and therefore can change the final result, sometimes by a small amount and sometimes, in pathological cases involving catastrophic cancellation, by a great deal.

This lack of associativity becomes especially relevant in large matrix multiplications, where each output element is the sum of potentially thousands or millions of products. On modern hardware, such reductions are almost never carried out in a single fixed sequence. GPUs and CPUs exploit parallelism, using multiple threads, vector lanes, or specialized tensor cores that split the summation into partial sums computed in parallel and then combined, often in a tree-like pattern rather than a strict left-to-right order. The number of threads, the tile sizes chosen by a kernel, the specific hardware architecture, the compiler's instruction scheduling, and even runtime factors like which order thread blocks happen to finish in can all alter the grouping of the additions. Since each different grouping is a different, mathematically distinct sequence of roundings, the results can differ in the last few bits, or occasionally more significantly, from one run to another or from one hardware platform to another, even when the same high-level algorithm and the same input data are used.

For most numerical applications, these discrepancies are negligible, sitting near the level of floating-point epsilon. But they matter for reproducibility: two runs of the same matrix multiplication on different GPUs, different library versions, or even different thread counts on the same GPU may produce bit-for-bit different outputs. This complicates scientific reproducibility, debugging, and validation of machine learning training pipelines, where downstream computations, such as many layers of a neural network or iterative solvers, can amplify these tiny discrepancies into meaningfully divergent results over time, making exact bitwise reproducibility very difficult to guarantee without deliberately sacrificing performance by fixing the reduction order.

Floating-point numbers are a finite subset of the reals, and each arithmetic operation must return a value drawn from that subset. When two IEEE 754 doubles are added, the exact mathematical sum is computed conceptually and then rounded to the nearest representable value, which introduces an error of up to half an unit in the last place of the result. Because rounding happens after every operation rather than once at the end, the order in which sums are accumulated determines where and how much information is discarded. Consider adding a large number, a small number, and the negation of the large number. If the two large magnitudes are combined first, they cancel exactly and the small value survives intact. If instead the small value is added to the large one first, it may be entirely absorbed, since the exact sum requires more significand bits than the format provides, and the final subtraction then yields zero. Both results are correctly rounded at each step; they simply differ, which is precisely the statement that addition is not associative. Subtractive cancellation, absorption, and the accumulation of many small rounding errors in a long running sum are the mechanisms by which the discrepancy grows, and the worst-case relative error of a naive sequential sum grows roughly with the number of terms times the machine epsilon, whereas pairwise or blocked summation grows only logarithmically.

Matrix multiplication is nothing but a large collection of dot products, each of which is a reduction over the inner dimension. High-performance implementations never perform those reductions in the naive left-to-right order. They tile the computation to fit cache hierarchies, split the inner dimension across multiple threads or GPU blocks and combine partial sums afterwards, use vector registers so that several independent accumulators run in parallel and are merged at the end, and sometimes employ fused multiply-add instructions that skip an intermediate rounding altogether or higher-precision accumulators for lower-precision inputs. Each of these choices imposes a different association of the same additions, so each produces a slightly different, equally defensible answer. The practical consequences are that changing thread count, tile size, hardware generation, library version, or even the arrival order of asynchronous partial results can perturb the output in the last few bits. Those perturbations are usually harmless, but they can be amplified by ill-conditioned problems, by iterative algorithms that feed outputs back as inputs, or by discrete decisions such as comparisons and argmax, turning a bit-level difference into a visibly different outcome. Achieving reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order or using compensated and exactly-rounded summation techniques, generally at some cost in speed.

Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers with a fixed, finite number of significant bits (typically 24 for single precision or 53 for double precision, following the IEEE 754 standard). When two floating-point numbers of different magnitudes are added, the smaller number must be shifted so its exponent matches the larger one, and in the process, some of its least significant bits may fall off the end and be rounded away. This rounding step means the result of an addition is only an approximation of the true mathematical sum, accurate to the precision of the format but not exact. Because each addition introduces its own small rounding error, the order in which numbers are summed determines which intermediate values get rounded and how, so (a + b) + c can yield a different bit pattern than a + (b + c), even though both are mathematically equal in real-number arithmetic. This is fundamentally different from real-number addition, where grouping never matters.

This lack of associativity becomes significant in large matrix multiplications, where each output element is computed as the sum of many products—potentially thousands or millions of terms for large matrices. The final rounded result depends on the order in which those products are accumulated. On modern hardware, this order is rarely fixed or predictable. GPUs and multi-core CPUs parallelize the summation across many threads or cores, splitting the terms into chunks that are reduced independently and then combined; the number of chunks, their sizes, and the order in which partial sums are combined can vary depending on the hardware, the number of threads used, the specific kernel or library implementation, or even runtime scheduling decisions. Vectorized instructions (like SIMD or tensor cores) may also group elements differently depending on alignment and batch size. As a result, running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, with a different number of GPU streaming multiprocessors, a different thread count, or even a different software library version, can produce numerically different results at the level of the least significant bits, despite using the same input data and the same nominal algorithm.

This has practical consequences for reproducibility. Scientific computations, machine learning training runs, and numerical simulations that rely on matrix multiplication may not produce bit-identical outputs across different machines, GPU models, or parallelization strategies, even though the differences are tiny at each individual step. Over many operations, especially in iterative processes like neural network training, these tiny discrepancies can compound, leading to divergent trajectories, different final model weights, or different simulation outcomes, making exact reproducibility across hardware configurations difficult without deliberately constraining the reduction order or using higher-precision or deterministic accumulation strategies.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity in Matrix Multiplication

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware does not satisfy the mathematical property of associativity, meaning that (a + b) + c may not equal a + (b + c). This fundamental limitation stems from how processors represent numbers using a fixed number of bits and the rounding rules that govern arithmetic operations.

When a computer performs floating-point addition, it must represent the result in a finite format, typically using IEEE 754 double-precision or single-precision standards. These formats allocate a fixed number of bits to the mantissa or significant digits, constraining the precision to roughly sixteen decimal digits for double-precision numbers. When two numbers of very different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's least significant digits may fall outside the representable precision range and are discarded through rounding. This rounding process is deterministic for a given pair of inputs, but it means that adding numbers in different orders produces different rounding errors that accumulate differently.

Consider adding three numbers where magnitudes differ significantly. If we compute (a + b) + c, the intermediate sum of a and b rounds to a representable value, and then c is added to this rounded result. Conversely, computing a + (b + c) first rounds b + c, then adds a to that different intermediate result. Although each operation individually follows IEEE standards, the sequence of rounding errors differs, and these errors do not cancel out. The final results can differ in the last few representable digits.

This property becomes critical when multiplying large matrices, where each element in the result matrix requires summing many partial products. A matrix multiplication of dimension n produces each output element by summing n intermediate products. When these sums are computed with different reduction orders—whether rows or columns are accumulated first, whether partial sums are combined in a tree structure or sequentially, or whether operations are parallelized differently—the order of floating-point additions changes.

On modern multi-core processors and GPUs, this variability is amplified. Parallel execution may sum elements in unpredictable orders depending on thread scheduling, communication patterns, and cache behavior. Even on a single machine, different parallelization strategies yield different accumulated rounding errors. Worse, the same code may produce different results when run multiple times if task scheduling varies slightly.

This non-associativity has profound implications for reproducibility. Scientific computations requiring bit-for-bit identical results across different execution contexts become impossible without special precautions. Developers pursuing reproducible results must either serialize computations to enforce a single reduction order, use higher precision for intermediate calculations, or employ compensated summation algorithms that track and correct rounding errors. Without such interventions, large matrix multiplications remain fundamentally non-reproducible across different hardware configurations or parallel execution strategies, even when using identical algorithms and input data.

Mathematically, real number addition is associative, meaning (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c), but with floating-point rounding, these two expressions can yield different results because the intermediate sum in each grouping is rounded differently before the next addition takes place. Over a long chain of additions, these small discrepancies can accumulate or cancel in unpredictable ways depending on the sequence of operations.

This lack of associativity becomes especially significant in large matrix multiplications, where each output element is computed as the sum of many products, often thousands or millions in deep learning or scientific computing contexts. The order in which these products are summed depends heavily on the underlying hardware and software implementation: GPUs, for instance, parallelize reductions across many threads and cores, and the specific grouping of partial sums depends on the number of threads, the tiling strategy, the memory layout, and even runtime scheduling decisions that can vary between library versions, hardware generations, or even repeated runs on the same machine. For most practical applications, these differences are negligible, since they lie within the expected numerical noise floor of floating-point computation. However, for reproducibility, especially in scientific research, regulatory validation, or debugging of machine learning training pipelines, such nondeterminism can be problematic. Two independent runs of a supposedly identical experiment on different GPUs or with different parallelization strategies may produce slightly different results, which can compound over iterative processes such as neural network training, potentially leading to divergent outcomes over time. This has motivated the development of deterministic algorithms and reproducibility-focused libraries that fix the reduction order or use higher-precision accumulation to minimize these discrepancies, though often at some cost to performance.

Matrix multiplication is nothing but a very large collection of dot products, and each dot product is a summation whose order is an implementation choice rather than a mathematical property. High-performance libraries split the reduction dimension into blocks sized to fit cache lines and registers, accumulate several partial sums in parallel to hide instruction latency, use fused multiply-add instructions that skip one rounding step, and on GPUs distribute the reduction across threads, warps, and blocks that combine their partial results in an order determined by scheduling and atomic operation arrival times. Change the number of threads, the tile size, the vector width, the library version, the hardware generation, or whether tensor cores with different internal accumulation precision are used, and the grouping of additions changes with it. The result is that two runs which are mathematically identical produce bitwise different matrices, typically differing in the last few significand bits.

For most numerical work these differences are harmless, but they break bitwise reproducibility, which matters when regression tests compare outputs exactly, when debugging requires deterministic replay, when iterative or chaotic computations amplify tiny perturbations over many steps, or when a threshold comparison flips and changes control flow. Remedies include fixed reduction orders, deterministic library modes, compensated or exact summation, and higher-precision accumulation, all of which trade performance for consistency.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware violates the mathematical property of associativity due to the finite precision inherent in how numbers are represented and combined. Unlike exact arithmetic where (a + b) + c always equals a + (b + c), floating-point operations round intermediate results to fit within the limited number of bits available for mantissa storage. When three numbers are added in different orders, the rounding errors accumulate differently, leading to distinct final results.

The root cause lies in how floating-point addition works. When two numbers are added, the hardware aligns their exponents, performs the addition on the mantissas, and then rounds the result to the nearest representable value. This rounding step discards information about less significant digits. Consider adding a very large number, a moderate number, and a very small number. If the small number is added to the large number first, it may be entirely lost in rounding because it becomes insignificant compared to the large number's magnitude. However, if the small and moderate numbers are added first, their sum might have sufficient magnitude to remain partially visible when added to the large number later. The order truly matters.

This non-associativity becomes critically important when performing large matrix multiplications, which fundamentally consist of computing many dot products—sums of products of corresponding elements. A single dot product involves adding potentially millions of terms, and the order in which these terms are summed directly influences the final result. When different computational strategies are employed, such as varying the order in which rows, columns, or blocks of matrices are processed, the accumulation order changes, and the rounding errors propagate differently.

# Floating-Point Addition and Non-Associativity in Matrix Multiplication

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware deviates from exact mathematics in fundamental ways, and one of the most consequential is the non-associativity of addition. This property emerges directly from the finite precision representation used by computers to approximate real numbers. When you add three numbers in floating-point, the result of computing (a + b) + c generally differs from a + (b + c) because intermediate rounding errors accumulate differently depending on the order of operations.

The IEEE 754 standard that governs floating-point computation on virtually all modern processors specifies that each arithmetic operation produces a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value. When you add two numbers, if their sum cannot be exactly represented in the available bits, the result gets rounded. This rounding error is small for any single operation, but when you perform millions or billions of additions in sequence, the order in which you combine values profoundly affects the accumulated error.

Consider a simple example: adding a very large number to a very small number repeatedly. If you add the small numbers together first before adding the large number, you accumulate their contribution before encountering cancellation effects. If you add them one at a time to an ever-growing sum, many of the small numbers may be entirely lost to rounding, their magnitude insufficient to alter the large number within the precision available.

Matrix multiplication involves a massive reduction problem: each element of the output matrix is computed by taking the dot product of a row and column, which requires summing many intermediate products. When you multiply large matrices, you face a choice about reduction order, even though mathematically all orders should produce the same result. You could sum the products left-to-right, use a tree-structured reduction that minimizes intermediate magnitudes, or adopt various other strategies. Each produces a numerically different answer.

This non-associativity becomes a critical problem for reproducibility. If a team of researchers computes a matrix multiplication on one system, then attempts to reproduce that result on another system with different hardware or compiler settings, the reduction order may change. Different CPU architectures might apply different instruction-level parallelism strategies. Different compilers might reorder operations to optimize performance. Two identical-looking matrix multiplication calls can produce different floating-point results.

For scientific computing, this poses a genuine dilemma. Users want bit-for-bit reproducible results to verify algorithms and ensure consistency across platforms. Yet achieving reproducibility requires sacrificing some performance benefits that modern hardware offers through parallel reduction. The problem intensifies with larger matrices, where more rounding errors accumulate and more opportunities exist for different reduction orderings. Many projects now accept that reproducibility requires either mandating specific reduction orders at the cost of performance, or accepting that floating-point results are inherently platform-dependent within some acceptable tolerance.

Because rounding is a nonlinear operation—small perturbations in an operand can shift the result to a different representable number—these two computations can produce distinct final results even though the underlying real-number arithmetic is associative. This is not a bug or a hardware defect; it is an unavoidable consequence of representing infinite precision with finitely many bits, as codified in the IEEE 754 standard, which specifies correctly rounded results for individual operations but says nothing about the order in which a sequence of operations should be performed.

This complicates debugging, testing, and scientific reproducibility, and has motivated efforts to provide deterministic modes in deep learning frameworks, even though such modes often sacrifice some performance to enforce a fixed reduction order.

# Floating-Point Addition and Non-Associativity in Matrix Multiplication

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware deviates from pure mathematics in fundamental ways, most notably in the violation of associativity for addition. This property—or rather, its absence—creates significant practical challenges when performing large numerical computations like matrix multiplication.

The root cause lies in the finite precision of floating-point representation. Modern computers typically use IEEE 754 double-precision format, which stores numbers with only 53 bits of precision. When adding two floating-point numbers, the result is rounded to fit within this limited precision. The crucial point is that the order of operations matters because rounding errors accumulate differently depending on which numbers are combined first.

Consider adding three numbers: a very large number, a medium number, and a very small number. If we first add the large and small numbers, the small number may be lost entirely due to rounding—its bits fall below the precision threshold when combined with the magnitude of the large number. However, if we first add the two smaller numbers to create a relatively larger value, more of that magnitude survives into the final sum. Mathematically these should be identical, but computationally they produce different results.

This non-associativity becomes particularly problematic in matrix multiplication at scale. A matrix multiplication operation fundamentally involves computing dot products, where each element is formed by summing many products. The number of terms in these sums grows with matrix dimension. When computing the same matrix product with different computational strategies—whether by processing rows first or columns first, or by partitioning the work among different processors—the order in which partial products are accumulated changes. Each different reduction order produces slightly different rounding errors.

On modern parallel hardware, this problem intensifies. Different processors may compute partial sums independently and then combine them, but the order of combination is often non-deterministic or depends on runtime scheduling. Floating-point addition on one processor followed by communication and addition on another processor will not necessarily yield the same result as a different ordering, even if all arithmetic is correctly implemented according to standards.

For large matrices, these errors compound significantly. A matrix multiplication of two thousand-by-thousand matrices involves billions of floating-point operations. The accumulated rounding errors can become substantial enough that results vary measurably depending on execution parameters. This creates genuine reproducibility challenges: running the same computation twice may yield slightly different results, not due to hardware faults or software bugs, but due to the inherent mathematical properties of finite-precision arithmetic combined with non-deterministic scheduling in parallel systems.

These limitations matter greatly in scientific computing, machine learning, and high-performance computing generally, where reproducibility and numerical reliability are essential for validation and debugging.

Some domains, particularly high-performance computing and scientific simulation, have developed workarounds including ordered reduction algorithms and careful control over computation order. Change the grouping and you change which intermediate magnitudes meet, and therefore which rounding errors occur and how large they are. The individual discrepancies are tiny, usually on the order of the accumulated rounding error, but they are not noise to be ignored: iterative solvers, training loops, and branching logic can amplify them until trajectories visibly diverge. # Floating-Point Addition and Associativity in Matrix Multiplication

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers does not satisfy the mathematical property of associativity, meaning that the order in which you add numbers affects the final result. This departure from ideal mathematics has profound implications for scientific computing, particularly when performing large matrix multiplications where billions of arithmetic operations accumulate numerical errors.

The fundamental cause lies in how floating-point numbers are represented and manipulated. Modern hardware uses IEEE 754 standard floating-point numbers, which store values with limited precision using a fixed number of bits. A 64-bit double-precision number dedicates some bits to a mantissa (the significant digits) and some to an exponent, allowing representation of a wide range of magnitudes. However, only about 15 significant decimal digits can be stored accurately. When two numbers of very different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's least significant bits may be completely lost due to rounding. Consequently, (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) when the magnitudes involved vary significantly.

Consider a simple example: adding a very large number, a moderate number, and a tiny number. If you first add the large and tiny numbers, the tiny number essentially disappears during rounding because the large number's exponent dominates. But if you add the moderate and tiny numbers first, you might preserve more information before adding to the large number. The order of operations determines which information survives the inevitable rounding.

In matrix multiplication, the problem becomes acute because the algorithm fundamentally requires summing many products together. A single element of the resulting matrix typically requires summing thousands or millions of terms. Different parallel implementations may reduce these partial sums in different orders: one thread might accumulate results left-to-right, another might use a tree-structured reduction, and a third might employ a different blocking strategy. Each approach produces slightly different rounding errors, yielding different final answers.

For small problems, these differences may be negligible, remaining in the least significant bits. But for large matrix multiplications common in deep learning and scientific simulation, accumulated rounding errors can become visible. Two runs of the same computation on different hardware, using different libraries, or even with different numbers of parallel threads can produce results that differ beyond acceptable tolerances, making reproducibility difficult.

This non-associativity is not a bug but a fundamental consequence of finite-precision arithmetic. Practitioners address it by accepting some irreproducibility as inevitable, using higher precision arithmetic when necessary, employing compensated summation algorithms that track rounding errors, or requiring tests to check numerical proximity rather than exact equality. Understanding this limitation has become essential for anyone writing or deploying large-scale numerical software.

This has real implications for scientific computing, debugging, and machine learning, where researchers may struggle to exactly reproduce training results or benchmark comparisons, and where accumulated rounding differences can compound across many layers of computation, especially in deep neural networks trained over millions of iterations.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers does not obey the mathematical property of associativity, meaning that the order in which you add numbers affects the final result. This seemingly simple fact has profound implications for scientific computing, particularly when performing large matrix multiplications.

The root cause lies in how floating-point numbers are represented and manipulated in hardware. Modern computers use the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers with a fixed number of bits for the mantissa or significand, typically 53 bits for double precision. When two floating-point numbers are added, the hardware must align their binary representations and then perform the addition. However, the result often cannot be represented exactly in the available bits, so it must be rounded. This rounding introduces a tiny error that is unavoidable and fundamental to the system.

Consider what happens when you add three numbers in two different orders. If you compute (a + b) + c versus a + (b + c), the intermediate rounding operations differ. When you first add a and b, any error introduced by rounding affects how this intermediate result interacts with c. A different grouping means different intermediate results with different rounding errors, ultimately producing different final answers. The differences are small—typically on the order of machine epsilon, which is around 10^-16 for double precision—but they are measurable and deterministic.

Matrix multiplication involves a massive number of floating-point operations, especially for large matrices. A matrix product requires many dot products, and each dot product is essentially a sum of products. If you perform these operations in a different order—perhaps due to different parallelization strategies, different processor scheduling, or deliberate algorithmic choices—the accumulation of rounding errors takes different paths. These divergent paths can compound through the computation, amplifying small differences into noticeable variation.

This loss of reproducibility becomes critical in scientific and engineering applications where results must be verified or validated across different computing platforms or over time. The same code run twice on different hardware architectures, or even with different compiler optimizations, can produce slightly different results. For many applications, this imprecision is acceptable and expected. However, in domains like weather prediction, climate modeling, or financial simulations, practitioners often require bit-for-bit reproducibility to ensure their results are trustworthy and debuggable.

The challenge intensifies with parallel computing. When matrix operations are distributed across multiple processors, the reduction order—the sequence in which partial results are combined—becomes another source of non-determinism. Different load balancing decisions lead to different reduction orders, which lead to different final answers.

Understanding this limitation is essential for modern scientific computing. Programmers must choose between speed, through arbitrary reduction orders enabled by parallelization, and reproducibility, through controlled, sequential reduction orders that sacrifice performance but guarantee consistent results.

This non-reproducibility presents a genuine challenge for scientific computing. # Floating-Point Addition and Associativity in Matrix Multiplication

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware deviates from the mathematical properties we expect from real numbers, most notably in the failure of associativity. This fundamental difference stems from the finite precision representation used by computers to store decimal numbers. According to the IEEE 754 standard, floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of bits for the significand and exponent, typically 53 bits for double precision. When two numbers are added, the result is rounded to fit within this precision constraint, and this rounding can introduce small errors that accumulate in unexpected ways depending on the order of operations.

The non-associativity of floating-point addition means that (a + b) + c may not equal a + (b + c), even though these expressions are mathematically identical. This occurs because when adding three numbers in different orders, the intermediate results may round differently. For example, if a is extremely large and b and c are small, adding b to a first might lose information about b entirely due to rounding, whereas adding b and c together first could preserve their combined effect before addition to a. The order in which operations occur fundamentally changes which bits get rounded away and which are preserved.

This property directly impacts the reproducibility of large matrix multiplications, which compute results by accumulating many floating-point products into sums. A matrix multiplication result is typically computed by taking the dot product of rows and columns, which involves repeatedly adding products together. The order in which these products are accumulated significantly affects the final result. If one parallel computing system accumulates products in row-major order while another uses column-major order, or if one system groups products into smaller batches than another before summing, the rounding errors will accumulate differently and produce measurably different final results.

Modern processors compound this problem through their use of pipelining and out-of-order execution, which can further alter the order in which floating-point operations are actually performed compared to their order in the source code. Some systems may even use different precision levels in intermediate calculations, such as carrying extra bits in floating-point accumulators before rounding back to standard precision.

This non-reproducibility is not a bug but an inherent consequence of finite precision arithmetic combined with the commutativity achieved through different ordering strategies. For scientific computing, this creates significant challenges when comparing results across systems or when attempting to create deterministic behavior in parallel computations. Researchers have developed techniques like compensated summation and careful ordering strategies to mitigate these effects, but perfect reproducibility across all possible hardware configurations remains impractical without sacrificing performance.

# Floating-Point Addition and Non-Associativity in Matrix Multiplication

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware deviates from the mathematical ideal in fundamental ways. Unlike the real numbers, where addition is associative—meaning that grouping terms differently does not change the result—floating-point addition produces different results depending on the order in which operations occur.

This non-associativity arises from the finite precision of floating-point representation. Every floating-point number is stored with a limited number of bits, which means that real numbers must be rounded to fit this representation. When two floating-point numbers are added, the result is computed and then rounded again to fit within the available precision. If one operand is much larger than the other, the smaller operand's contribution may be entirely lost due to rounding, a phenomenon called catastrophic cancellation. Crucially, the order in which you add three or more numbers matters because earlier operations determine the intermediate values that govern subsequent rounding decisions.

Consider adding three numbers where one is very large and two are small. If you add the two small numbers first, their sum might be rounded to a tiny value before being added to the large number, potentially losing information. Conversely, if you add the small numbers to the large number sequentially, different rounding occurs at each step, yielding a different final result. Both answers are "correct" according to floating-point rules, yet they differ.

This problem becomes acute in matrix multiplication, one of the most fundamental operations in scientific computing. Matrix multiplication involves computing dot products, which sum many products together. The order of accumulation directly affects which rounding operations occur and thus the final result. When the same matrix multiplication is executed with different reduction orders—different ways of grouping and ordering the accumulated sums—the floating-point results diverge.

On modern hardware with multiple processors or specialized accelerators, achieving a specific reduction order is difficult and expensive. Different processor counts, different parallel scheduling strategies, or even non-deterministic thread scheduling can cause the same matrix multiplication to follow different reduction paths. This means that running the same computation twice on the same hardware may produce slightly different numerical results.

The reproducibility problem is particularly severe for large matrices because the accumulated rounding errors compound. Some applications can tolerate small numerical differences, but others cannot. Financial calculations, verification testing, and debugging all require deterministic results. Researchers addressing this challenge often resort to using special reduction algorithms that enforce specific ordering, using higher precision arithmetic than strictly necessary, or accepting that bit-perfect reproducibility is incompatible with high performance on modern parallel hardware. The tension between floating-point efficiency and reproducibility remains a significant practical concern in scientific computing.

Because grouping changes which intermediate sums are formed, it changes which roundings occur, and the accumulated errors differ. The classic illustration uses a large value and two small ones: adding 10^16 to 1 in double precision leaves 10^16 unchanged, because the exact answer falls between adjacent representable values and rounds back down, so (10^16 + 1) − 10^16 yields zero while 10^16 + (1 − 10^16) yields one. Nothing here is a hardware defect; each individual operation is correctly rounded, and it is precisely that per-operation rounding that destroys associativity. Related effects include catastrophic cancellation, where subtracting nearly equal quantities exposes error that earlier roundings had hidden, and absorption, where small addends vanish entirely against a large running total. Distributivity fails for analogous reasons, and extended-precision accumulators, fused multiply-add instructions, and compiler reassociation under fast-math flags all shift the pattern of roundings without eliminating the underlying sensitivity.

When large matrix multiplications are executed with different reduction orders, the results can differ noticeably, especially as matrices grow larger. One reduction order might accumulate rounding errors differently than another, leading to measurably different outputs. This becomes particularly acute in distributed computing environments, where different processors might perform reductions in different orders based on load balancing or communication patterns.

The reproducibility challenge is severe for scientific applications requiring exact results. For instance, if researchers run the same simulation on different hardware or with different parallelization strategies, they may obtain slightly different results purely due to different floating-point reduction orders. This makes debugging difficult and complicates verification of results across computational platforms.

Various solutions exist, including careful ordering of operations to minimize error accumulation, using higher-precision intermediate computations, or implementing compensated summation algorithms that track and correct rounding errors. However, these approaches introduce computational overhead. Understanding floating-point non-associativity is essential for anyone working with numerical computing, as it explains why reproducibility cannot be guaranteed without explicitly controlling operation ordering.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so most real values cannot be represented exactly. A double-precision number carries roughly fifteen to seventeen significant decimal digits, and every arithmetic operation must round its exact mathematical result back into that representable set. Addition is where this rounding becomes visibly order-dependent. When two numbers of very different magnitudes are added, the smaller one must be shifted right to align exponents, and bits that fall off the end of the significand are lost. Consider the classic example of adding one, then ten to the twentieth, then negative ten to the twentieth. Adding one to a quantity as large as ten to the twentieth changes nothing, because the one is far below the last representable bit, so the sum is ten to the twentieth, and subtracting it leaves zero. Reorder the operands so that the two enormous values cancel first, and the remaining sum is exactly one. Both computations are individually correct in the sense that each rounding was the nearest representable value, yet the answers differ by the entire magnitude of the smaller operand. Associativity fails not because the hardware is defective but because rounding is a nonlinear function inserted after every operation, and function composition in a different order gives a different result.

Matrix multiplication is nothing but a very large collection of sums, since each output element is a dot product of a row and a column. The mathematical definition says nothing about the order in which those products are accumulated, and high-performance implementations exploit that freedom aggressively. A single-threaded naive loop accumulates strictly left to right. A blocked or tiled implementation splits the dot product into chunks that fit in cache, accumulates partial sums within each chunk, and then combines the chunk totals. A vectorized kernel maintains several independent accumulators, one per lane of a SIMD register, and merges them at the end. A multithreaded or GPU implementation may split the inner dimension across many workers whose partial results arrive in whatever order the scheduler produces, and tensor cores or fused multiply-add units may keep intermediate products at different precision than the surrounding arithmetic. Each of these strategies is a different parenthesization of the same mathematical sum, so each can yield a slightly different floating-point answer.

The practical consequence is that the same source code, the same inputs, and the same nominal precision can produce bitwise different outputs when the thread count changes, when the library selects a different kernel for a different matrix shape, when hardware with wider vectors is used, or simply when nondeterministic atomic accumulation reorders arrivals between runs. Individual discrepancies are tiny, near the unit of least precision, but iterative algorithms and long training runs amplify them until trajectories diverge visibly. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, which usually costs performance.

When two floating-point numbers of very different magnitudes are added, the smaller number must be shifted so its exponent matches the larger one, and in that shifting process, some of its low-order bits fall off the end and are lost to rounding. Because the amount of information lost depends on the relative magnitudes and signs of the two operands being combined at that moment, the result of (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) whenever intermediate sums have different magnitudes in the two groupings. Mathematically, real-number addition is associative, but floating-point addition is only an approximation of that ideal, and the approximation error is order-dependent.

This matters enormously for large matrix multiplications because computing each output element requires summing potentially thousands or millions of products, and the order in which those products are summed is not fixed by the mathematical definition of matrix multiplication alone—it depends on the implementation. Consequently the same mathematical product computed by two libraries, by one library on two machines with different vector widths or core counts, or by the same code with a different tile size or thread count, will typically agree only to within a small relative error rather than bit for bit. The discrepancies are usually harmless in magnitude, but they break exact reproducibility, they can be amplified by ill-conditioned problems or long iterative computations such as training loops, and they complicate debugging and regression testing. Remedies include fixing the reduction tree deterministically, using compensated or extended-precision accumulation, or exactly reproducible summation algorithms, all at some cost in speed.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware follows the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers in a limited precision format. This fundamental constraint makes addition non-associative in practice, even though it is associative in mathematical theory. Understanding why this occurs and how it impacts scientific computing is crucial for anyone working with numerical algorithms at scale.

The core issue stems from the finite precision of floating-point representation. Every floating-point number occupies a fixed number of bits, typically 64 for double precision, which limits how many significant digits can be stored. When adding two numbers of vastly different magnitudes, the smaller number may be too tiny relative to the larger one to affect the result once both are rounded to the available precision. This phenomenon is called catastrophic cancellation or absorption.

Consider what happens when computing (a + b) + c versus a + (b + c). If a is very large and b and c are small but equal in magnitude to each other, the order matters. Adding b to a first might result in a being unchanged due to rounding, effectively losing b. Then adding c produces the same loss. However, if you add b and c together first, their sum might be large enough to affect a when added. The two orderings produce different results, violating the mathematical associativity we expect.

For large matrix multiplications, this non-associativity becomes increasingly problematic. A matrix multiplication requires accumulating the products of many elements, summing them in some order. The traditional approach processes elements row by row or in some other sequential pattern, but this choice of reduction order directly affects the final numerical result. Two different execution orders for the same multiplication will generally produce slightly different results due to different rounding errors accumulating at different points.

Modern hardware exacerbates this issue because parallel processors often compute partial sums in different threads and combine them in unpredictable orders. The operating system scheduler, memory access patterns, and even the specific processor cores assigned to a computation can influence which partial sums combine first. This means that running the identical matrix multiplication code twice on the same machine might produce slightly different answers if the computation is parallelized.

For scientific applications requiring reproducibility, this poses a significant challenge. Climate simulations, machine learning models, and financial computations often need to produce identical results when run multiple times or on different systems. To achieve this, programmers must either use serialized floating-point operations that prevent reordering, sacrifice performance by avoiding parallelization, or accept that exact reproducibility across platforms is mathematically impossible and instead verify results within acceptable numerical tolerances.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so each arithmetic result must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition of two IEEE 754 doubles is defined to produce the exactly correct sum rounded once to 53 significant bits; the operation itself is commutative, because the exact sum does not depend on operand order. Associativity fails, however, because chaining additions means rounding more than once, and the amount of information discarded at each rounding depends on the magnitudes involved. If you add a very large number to a very tiny one, the tiny one may fall entirely below the least significant bit of the larger and vanish; grouped differently, several tiny numbers might first accumulate into something large enough to survive. The canonical illustration is that with a large value L and a small value s, (L + s) − L can round to zero while L + (s − L) yields s exactly. Catastrophic cancellation is the mirror image: subtracting nearly equal quantities annihilates leading digits and promotes previously harmless rounding error into the leading digits of the result. So the sum of a list of floating-point numbers depends on the order and grouping in which the partial sums are formed, and the spread between the best and worst orderings grows with the length of the list and with the dynamic range of its terms.

Matrix multiplication is, at its core, a very large collection of dot products, and a dot product is a reduction — precisely the operation whose result depends on grouping. High-performance implementations never evaluate those reductions in the naive left-to-right order. They tile the computation for cache and register reuse, split the contraction dimension into blocks that are accumulated separately, use multiple independent accumulators to hide the latency of the fused multiply-add pipeline, exploit SIMD lanes that each hold a partial sum before a final horizontal combination, and on GPUs distribute slices of the contraction across threads, warps, or whole devices whose partial results are later combined by atomics or a tree reduction. Each of these choices imposes a different parenthesization. Consequently the same mathematical product, computed by the same library on the same data, can yield bitwise different results when the tile sizes change, when the number of threads changes, when the hardware dispatches a different kernel for a different problem shape, when a tensor-core path with different internal accumulation precision is selected, or when nondeterministic atomic ordering shuffles the combination of partial sums between runs.

The discrepancies are usually tiny relative to the magnitude of the entries, on the order of the unit roundoff times the accumulation length, but they are not nothing. Iterative algorithms amplify them, comparisons and branches turn them into qualitatively different control flow, and training runs diverge. Reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order — deterministic kernels, fixed thread counts, pinned library versions — or removing the dependence altogether through compensated summation, higher-precision or fixed-point accumulators, and similar techniques that make the answer insensitive to grouping.

This is why bitwise reproducibility of floating-point computations across different hardware, driver versions, or thread counts is difficult to guarantee: reproducing exact results requires fixing not just the mathematical operations but also the exact order of the underlying additions, which in turn requires controlling low-level implementation details that most software stacks do not expose or guarantee.

# Floating-Point Addition and the Loss of Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers follows the IEEE 754 standard, which deliberately trades perfect mathematical precision for speed and practicality. This design choice creates a fundamental problem: addition of floating-point numbers is not associative. That is, (a + b) + c does not necessarily equal a + (b + c) when these values are represented in binary floating-point format.

The root cause lies in how floating-point numbers are represented and combined. Each number occupies a fixed number of bits, with some devoted to the exponent and others to the mantissa or significant digits. When adding two numbers of very different magnitudes, the smaller number's digits may fall entirely outside the available precision, causing them to be rounded away. The order in which we perform additions therefore matters crucially.

Consider adding a large number, a tiny number, and another large number. If we first add the two large numbers together, their sum consumes the available precision. When we then add the tiny number, it may be too small relative to this huge intermediate result to affect any of the retained digits, so it vanishes entirely due to rounding. Conversely, if we added the tiny number to one of the large numbers first, we might lose it then, but perhaps recover a different portion of its value in subsequent operations. The final result depends entirely on the sequence of operations.

This non-associativity becomes catastrophic when multiplying large matrices. Matrix multiplication involves accumulating many products into a single result, and the order in which these accumulated products are added determines the final numerical result. Different reduction strategies produce different answers. For instance, multiplying a matrix with 1000 columns requires summing 1000 products. We might add these left-to-right sequentially, or we might split them into groups and add the groups hierarchically, or use various other tree-based reduction patterns.

When the same matrix multiplication runs on different hardware, with different numbers of processors, or even with different compiler optimizations, the reduction order changes. A GPU with 256 cores will naturally divide the work differently than a CPU with eight cores, leading to entirely different intermediate sums and ultimately different final results. This is not a bug but an inevitable consequence of the mathematical model underlying floating-point computation.

For scientific computing, this creates severe reproducibility challenges. The same computation cannot be guaranteed to produce identical results across different platforms or even different runs on the same platform. Researchers have responded by developing specialized libraries that enforce consistent reduction orders, or by using higher-precision arithmetic for intermediate results. Understanding this limitation is essential for anyone working with large-scale numerical computation, as the difference between results can exceed acceptable tolerances even when all computations are performed correctly according to IEEE 754 standards.

Tensor cores and fused multiply-add instructions add further variation, since a fused operation rounds once instead of twice and may internally use wider precision.

Each of these strategies computes a differently parenthesized version of the same mathematical sum, so each can produce a slightly different result. The discrepancies are usually near the level of rounding error, but they are not noise to be ignored: they grow with the length of the reduction, they grow much larger when terms cancel, and in iterative computations they can be amplified until trajectories diverge visibly. Consequently the same program can yield different numbers on different hardware, with different thread counts, with different library versions, or after autotuning selects a new kernel. Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, which generally costs performance, or using compensated or extended-precision accumulation to make the result insensitive to that order.
